messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
A metric space $(M, d)$ is complete if and only if it satisfies the specified nested set condition. This equivalence links topological completeness with the behavior of shrinking closed sets.

Consider the forward direction first. Suppose $(M, d)$ is complete. Let $(F_n)$ be a sequence of nonempty closed subsets such that $F_{n+1} \subset F_n$ and $\text{diam}(F_n) \to 0$. We must show $\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} F_n \neq \emptyset$. Since each $F_n$ is nonempty, we can select an element $x_n \in F_n$ for every $n$. Because the sets are nested, $x_n \in F_k$ for all $k \le n$.

For any indices $m < n$, both points $x_m$ and $x_n$ belong to $F_m$. Therefore, the distance between them is bounded by the diameter of $F_m$:
$$ d(x_m, x_n) \le \text{diam}(F_m) $$
As $n \to \infty$, we also have $m \to \infty$ eventually. Since $\text{diam}(F_m) \to 0$, it follows that for any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $N$ such that for all $m, n \ge N$, $d(x_m, x_n) < \epsilon$. Thus, $(x_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence.

Since $M$ is complete, the sequence $(x_n)$ converges to some limit point $x \in M$. We now verify that $x$ lies in every $F_k$. Fix an arbitrary $k$. For all $n \ge k$, we have $x_n \in F_k$. Since $F_k$ is closed and contains the tail of the sequence $(x_n)_{n \ge k}$, it must contain the limit $x$. Hence, $x \in F_k$ for all $k$, which implies $x \in \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} F_n$. The intersection is nonempty.

Now consider the reverse direction. Assume that any sequence of nonempty closed sets satisfying the nested and shrinking diameter conditions has a nonempty intersection. We must prove that $(M, d)$ is complete. Let $(x_n)$ be an arbitrary Cauchy sequence in $M$. Define the set $F_n$ as the closure of the tail of the sequence:
$$ F_n = \overline{\{x_k : k \ge n\}} $$
Each $F_n$ is closed by definition. Since the sets are tails, $\{x_k : k \ge n+1\} \subset \{x_k : k \ge n\}$, which implies $F_{n+1} \subset F_n$. The sequence $(x_n)$ is Cauchy, meaning for any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $N$ such that $d(x_i, x_j) < \epsilon$ for all $i, j \ge N$. Consequently, the diameter of the set $\{x_k : k \ge n\}$ becomes arbitrarily small as $n \to \infty$. Since the diameter of a closure equals the diameter of the original set in metric spaces, we have $\text{diam}(F_n) \to 0$.

By our assumption, the intersection $\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} F_n$ is nonempty. Let $x$ be an element in this intersection. Then $x \in F_n$ for all $n$, which means $x \in \overline{\{x_k : k \ge n\}}$. This implies that the distance from $x$ to the set $\{x_k : k \ge n\}$ is zero, so there exists some index $k_n \ge n$ such that $d(x, x_{k_n}) < 1/n$. As $n \to \infty$, $d(x, x_{k_n}) \to 0$. Since $(x_n)$ is Cauchy and has a subsequence converging to $x$, the entire sequence $(x_n)$ converges to $x$. Thus, every Cauchy sequence in $M$ converges, proving that $M$ is complete.

Therefore, the completeness of the metric space is equivalent to the nonemptiness of such nested intersections.
